extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and graduate mathematics students and enthusiasts interested in proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and producing concise, rigorous mathematical proofs that employ classical inequalities, valuation methods, diagonalization, and combinatorial/topological counting arguments; includes worked examples and strategies (Cauchy–Schwarz, AM–GM, p-adic valuations, Sperner-style counting, transfinite induction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonalization to separate cardinalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a diagonal set U = {m ∈ N : m ∉ φ(m)} to show that no bijection from M (or a subset N ⊆ M) onto P(M) can exist, yielding |P(M)| > |M|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the subset U of indices that are not contained in their image under a purported bijection ϕ, then derive the contradiction u ∈ U ⇔ u ∉ U. (Text uses the classical barber-riddle style diagonalization.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction by transfinite induction with diagonalization
rubrics_metrics.description: When building a family {f_β} indexed by countable ordinals, reorder earlier functions into a sequence g_n and points w_n and define f_γ by a power-series-like expansion f_γ(z)=Σ ε_n ∏_{i=1}^n (z−w_i) so that f_γ(w_n) can be chosen step-by-step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose coefficients ε_n inductively: values of ε_m for m ≥ n do not affect f_γ(w_n), so pick ε_n to satisfy value constraints (e.g. f_γ(w_n) ∈ dense set D and f_γ(w_n) ≠ g_n(w_n)). Ensure the sequence (ε_n) tends to 0 'sufficiently fast' so the series defines an analytic function. Use diagonalization on values to guarantee distinctness of constructed functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-ordering / initial ordinal arguments for cardinal comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Use well-orderings and the notion of initial ordinal ω_m to compare cardinal numbers and to establish existence of the 'next larger' cardinal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-order the index set according to its initial ordinal, consider initial segments W_μ, and use the smallest initial ordinal among a collection to pick minimal cardinals. These ordinal-technical steps are used to show existence of a definite next larger cardinal and to control constructions involving many countable sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling unions of many countable sets via well-ordering and replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: To show the union of a family {A_α} of size m of countable sets has size at most m, replace each index α by a countable disjoint set B_α and well-order the combined set to compare cardinalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume pairwise disjointness (only increases union size), well-order the index set by its initial ordinal ω_m, construct B_α = {b_{α1}=α, b_{α2},...} ordered by ω, then map these back to the A_α via bijections on countable subsequences. Use similarity/similarity-to-segment arguments to conclude |⋃A_α| ≤ m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quadratic expressions/discriminant to prove Cauchy–Schwarz
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove (a,b)^2 ≤ |a|^2|b|^2 by considering the quadratic function |x a + b|^2 in the real variable x and analyzing its discriminant; equality iff a and b are linearly dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume a ≠ 0. If b = λa equality is immediate. If linearly independent, |x a + b|^2 > 0 for all x, so the discriminant (a,b)^2 − |a|^2|b|^2 < 0, yielding the inequality. This exemplifies choosing a short 'Book Proof' via a suitable algebraic identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard induction strategy for AM–GM (doubling and reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality via two steps: (A) P(n) ⇒ P(n−1) and (B) P(n) and P(2) ⇒ P(2n), combined with base case P(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define P(n) as the desired inequality in a convenient algebraic form. For (A), use an auxiliary quantity A (a product or mean of n−1 terms) and compare. For (B), partition 2n variables into two groups and apply P(n) to each, then combine using P(2). This induction avoids standard direct convexity arguments and yields equality conditions as usual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted AM–GM via ordering and integral comparison (Alzer's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: For positive a_i and weights p_i summing to 1, bound the weighted geometric mean by the weighted arithmetic mean using ordering a_1 ≤ ... ≤ a_n, locating k with a_k ≤ G ≤ a_{k+1}, and deriving an integral inequality that yields A ≥ G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define G and A, exploit monotonicity to set up integrals of (t^{1/t} − 1)/t-type expressions, rewrite sums as integrals, and compare to get log inequalities. Analyze equality by checking when integrals vanish (all a_i equal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply inequalities to polynomial root-location problems by relating roots to coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate relationships among roots and coefficients (e.g., −a_{n−1} = sum of roots, a_{n−2} = pairwise sums) and apply Cauchy (or other) inequalities to bound individual roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express symmetric sums of roots, square or otherwise manipulate them, apply Cauchy–Schwarz or AM–GM to obtain quadratic inequalities in a chosen root y; solve to derive explicit interval bounds for roots and characterize equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use integral/AM–GM manipulations to bound geometric quantities of polynomials (Erdős–Gallai style)
rubrics_metrics.description: For polynomials with only real roots and specified boundary behavior (e.g., f(−1)=f(1)=0 and f>0 on (−1,1)), represent f(x) as (1−x^2)∏(α_i−x)(β_j+x) and apply AM–GM (and harmonic–geometric mean) in integral form to relate area A to tangential triangle area T and rectangle R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit symmetry x↦−x to average integrands and use AM–GM to pass to products like (α_i^2−x^2); compute f'(±1) explicitly and combine inequalities (and harmonic–geometric mean) to produce bounds such as (2/3)T ≤ A ≤ (2/3)R and analyze equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial counting plus inequalities for extremal graph bounds (Mantel/Turán)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bound the number of edges in triangle-free graphs by combining degree-sum double counting with Cauchy–Schwarz or AM–GM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let d_i be degrees, use di + dj ≤ n for each edge ij (no triangles), sum over edges to relate n|E| to Σ d_i^2, then apply Cauchy–Schwarz to get n|E| ≥ 4|E|^2 / n, concluding |E| ≤ n^2/4. Alternatively use maximal independent set size α, count edges incident to complement B and apply AM–GM: |E| ≤ Σ_{i∈B} d_i ≤ αβ ≤ (α+β)^2/4 = n^2/4. Check equality cases to characterize extremal graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: d'Alembert/Argand lemma technique for the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a nonconstant complex polynomial p(z) has a root, use d'Alembert's lemma: if p(a) ≠ 0 then every disc around a contains a point b with |p(b)| < |p(a)|, implying a global minimum of |p| must be zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write p(a+w)=p(a)+c w^m (1+r(w)) with minimal m≥1 and r(0)=0. Choose ζ an m-th root of −p(a)/|p(a)/c| (unit modulus) and w0=εζ with ε small so that |r(w0)|<1 and |c w0^m|<|p(a)|; deduce |p(a + w0)| < |p(a)|. Combine with continuity and Cauchy's minimum principle on a large disc to conclude the minimum of |p| is 0 (a root). Useful ingredients: continuity, existence of m-th roots on unit circle, and factorization of Taylor expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monsky's valuation-coloring method to obstruct equal-area odd dissections
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a 3-coloring of the plane using a non-Archimedean valuation v (extension of the 2-adic valuation with v(1/2) > 1) by coloring point (x,y) according to which of v(x), v(y), v(1) attains the maximum first; use valuation properties to force that any triangle with three different colors (a 'rainbow' triangle) has area whose v-value > 1 and hence cannot be 1/n for odd n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key valuation properties used: v(x+y) ≤ max{v(x),v(y)} and if v(x)≠v(y) then v(x+y)=max{v(x),v(y)}; also v(−x)=v(x), v(xy)=v(x)v(y). Prove the determinant built from coordinates of blue/green/red points has v-value ≥ 1 (so its area has v>1). Show any line gets at most two colors, and use a Sperner-style counting lemma to show any finite triangulation/dissection of the unit square contains an odd number of rainbow triangles, giving the contradiction for equal-area odd dissections. Note: existence of such a valuation (or an ordered-group-valued valuation with v(1/2)>1) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit non-Archimedean valuation algebraic consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a non-Archimedean valuation v, exploit v(x+y) ≤ max{v(x),v(y)} and the derived rule v(x+y)=max{v(x),v(y)} when v(x)≠v(y); also v(−x)=v(x) and multiplicativity hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties justify arguments comparing dominant diagonal summands vs. others in determinants (used in Monsky's lemma) and lead to sharp cancellation controls not available in Archimedean settings. They also imply v(a ± b1 ± ... ± bk)=v(a) if v(a) > v(b_i) for all i; use this to deduce when sums can't cancel in the valuation sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze equality cases to characterize extremal or sharp instances
rubrics_metrics.description: In each inequality-based proof, determine when equality occurs (e.g., Cauchy–Schwarz equality iff linear dependence; AM–GM equality iff all a_i equal; Mantel equality when graph is complete bipartite K_{n/2,n/2}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track equalities through each inequality application (discriminant zero, identical factors, or equality in AM–GM) to fully characterize extremal structures; often this completes the theorem by describing the only cases attaining bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic/strategic criterion: prefer short, conceptual 'Book Proofs'
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek elegant, short, conceptual proofs (so-called 'Book Proofs') that reveal structure and re-use classical inequalities in insightful ways, as illustrated by the examples and Pólya's commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for proofs that (i) exploit simple algebraic identities, (ii) reduce to known inequalities, (iii) use minimal machinery (continuity, basic valuation facts), and (iv) give transparent equality/structure analysis. The text repeatedly highlights such proofs as pedagogically and conceptually preferable.
